## Introduction
  The main goal of this project is to replicate the results from Experiment 2 of the Lopez-Brau & Ettinger (2023) paper. A secondary goal of this project is to partially replicate the results from Experiment 3a of the same paper. The paper broadly revolves around the inferences humans make about the social meaning of objects, specifically investigating whether adults are able to infer the communicative meaning of objects from their placement. Experiment 2 finds that adults believe that objects that impose a low cost on deciders are more likely to be communicative relative to objects that do not impose a cost. Experiment 3 furthers these findings: adults infer that a low-cost object in front of a door serves as a signal communicated by the person who placed the object that others should avoid that door. I anticipate leading projects on similar questions to investigate what inferences children make about the social meaning of objects. Replicating the methods and analysis will therefore be beneficial, serving as background findings motivating my studies and as a first step to brainstorming potential project designs and analysis plans for my own studies.  

  I anticipate the main challenges to be setting up the paradigm, specifically programming it using JavaScript which is unfamiliar to me. I imagine that it might be further challenging to code the study design such that failure on the attention checks reroutes participants to the start of the story and does not allow them to continue with the experiment until they pass the check (as per the published study design). I also anticipate collecting data from SONA to be challenging as the process is new to me.
  I hope to learn more about coding a jsPsych experiment and collecting data from an adult sample. Gaining skills in carrying out a jsPsych experiment and collecting data on SONA may both be helpful in the case I need to run or pilot studies on adult samples. Given some familiarity I have with running behavioral studies along with transparent materials and code provided by the authors, I am optimistic that this project will be feasible over the course of this quarter. More importantly, I hope to gain familiarity with how to replicate findings from a published project: from finding relevant materials and files from the original paper, to recreating the methods for data collection, all the way to rerunning the original analyses on my dataset and writing them up.
  
Link to my repository: https://github.com/anlaha/lopez-brau2023; Original Paper hosted on repository at: https://github.com/anlaha/lopez-brau2023/tree/main/original_paper 

## Methods

### Power Analysis

Original effect size, power analysis for samples to achieve 80%, 90%, 95% power to detect that effect size.  Considerations of feasibility for selecting planned sample size.
```{r}
library(pwr)

#original effect size of Exp 2
h.2 = ES.h(.725, .5)

#80% power to detect that effect
pwr.p.test(h = h.2, power = 0.8)$n
#90% power to detect that effect
pwr.p.test(h = h.2, power = 0.9)$n
#95% power to detect that effect
pwr.p.test(h = h.2, power = 0.95)$n

#original effect size of Exp 3
h.3 = ES.h(.8755, .5)

#80% power to detect that effect
pwr.p.test(h = h.3, power = 0.8)$n

#how much power would we have with the original sample size
pwr.p.test(h = h.2, n = 80)$power
```

### Planned Sample

The planned sample size is 80 participants recruited through UCSD SONA (to match the sample size of the original experiments). We would have 99% power to detect the effect size from the original Experiment 2.

### Materials

  All materials are hosted in the folder for the original project here: https://osf.io/57n4g/overview. There will be two parts of the replication project. The first part will include stimuli that consists of eight sets of images. Each set will have a pair of doors side-by-side: one “low-cost door” (object placed in front of the door) and one “no-cost door” (object placed beside the door). The objects will be a plant, a chair, a pile of books, a pile of cinderblocks, some tape, some meter sticks, a hat, and a fishbowl tied to a tack on a door frame. 

  The second part will include stimuli that consists of eight more images of pairs of doors, with each pair consisting
of an empty door and a door with an object placed directly in the middle of one of the doorways. Half of these door pairs will be open and the other half will be closed. The objects will be the same as listed above and participants will again be asked to imagine leaving an office and encountering this pair of doors. 

### Procedure	

  At the start of the experiment, participants will be asked to imagine leaving an office and encountering a pair of doors (the pair of doors in each trial will match the description as listed for each part of the experiment above). For the first part of the experiment, participants will complete eight sets of trials, each with a pair of images. For each set of images, they will be asked a series of multiple-choice questions: an attention-check (“What objects are in front of the doors?”), test trial (“Which door do you think someone was trying to tell you something?”), a manipulation check (“Which door requires more work to walk through?”) and lastly, an inclusion question (“Do you think you would be able to walk through this door if you wanted to?”). For the inclusion trial, we will only present a picture of the "low-cost door." Although this is a deviation from the original methods, we hope to minimize confusion for this trial. These methods will match the procedure from Experiment 2 of the paper. 

  For the second part of the experiment, participants will complete eight more sets of trials, each with a pair of images. Participants will then answer: an attention-check (“What is the only difference between the two exits?”), test trial (“What do you think someone was trying to tell you about the door with the object?”; the options provided will be (a) “You should walk through the door with the object” and (b) “You should not walk through the door with the object”), manipulation-check (same as Exp 2), and an inclusion question (same as Exp 2). For the inclusion trial, we will only present a picture of the "low-cost door." Although this is a deviation from the original methods, we hope to minimize confusion for this trial. These methods are a shortened version of the procedure from Experiment 3a of the paper (only including the "low-cost" condition) to account for time constraints of running the replication on SONA.

### Analysis Plan

  For the first part of the experiment (replication of Exp 2), trials in which participants fail the inclusion question will be excluded from the final dataset. For the second part of the experiment (replication of Exp 3a "low-cost" condition), trials in which participants fail either the inclusion question or the manipulation check will be excluded from the final dataset. The key analyses will be two-tailed binomial tests comparing participants' performance to chance (50%). We will also be conducting bootstrapped 95% CIs for these results.
  For the data collected in the first part of the study (replicating Exp 2 from the paper), participants' responses will be coded as 0 (choosing the "no-cost" door as more communicative) or 1 (choosing the "low-cost" door as more communicative). We will subset the data collected to measure their responses only to the first test trial (to match the number of trials in the original experiment). Participants' performance will then be compared to chance using a two-tailed binomial test to analyze whether participants chose the "low-cost" door as more communicative compared to the "no-cost" door.
  We will also run an exploratory test to measure participants' responses across the first part of the study. We will calculate the proportion of test-trials where they chose the "low-cost" door as more communicative and run a one-sample t-test to compare their performance to chance.
  For the second part of the study (replicating the "low-cost" condition from Exp 3a), participants' responses will be coded as 0 (choosing the door with no object as the one to avoid) or 1 (choosing the door with the object in front as the one to avoid). We will subset the data collected to measure their responses only to the first test trial (to match the number of trials in the original experiment). Participants' performance will again be compared to chance using a two-tailed binomial test to analyze whether participants chose the "low-cost" door as the one that was being used to communicate to others that it should be avoided. 
  We will again run an exploratory test to measure participants' responses across this second part of the study. We will calculate the proportion of test-trials where they chose the door with the object in front as the one to avoid and run a one-sample t-test to compare their performance to chance.
  Since we are not collecting new data for the "no-cost" condition, we will be comparing the the original data collected for that condition to the data we collect here in the first test trial of the second part of the study. We will conduct a Fisher’s exact test comparing participants' performance in the two conditions to investigate whether participants inferences of avoiding the door with the object was higher in the "low-cost"
condition compared to the "no-cost" condition.


### Differences from Original Study

  The most important difference here is that the current project will  be combining the procedures from Experiment 2 and part of Experiment 3a. Therefore, the data will be collected from the same sample of participants instead of two different samples (as in the original set of studies). It is possible that there may be order effects: participants' performance in identifying a "low-cost" door as more communicative (replication of Exp 2) could affect their performance in the trials involving participants' identification of the communicative goal in "low-cost" situations (replication of Exp 3a). There could also be other differences in the results in our replication attempt of the "low-cost" condition of Experiment 3a due to fatigue. 
  Another major difference here is that we will be having participants respond to all eight versions of test trials both when replicating Exp 2 and Exp 3a, compared to the one test trial run in the original studies. This is to account for the SONA study length requirements. This will also allow us to run a further exploratory test to examine our data. In addition to running a binomial test analyzing each participants' responses to the first test trial for each part of the experiment, we will run one-sample t-tests to analyze whether participants' proportion of responses for each eight set of trials differed from chance. 
  We have further slightly modified the stimuli presented for the inclusion question. The original study included the question "Do you think you would be able to walk through this door if you wanted to?" with the pictures of both doors, which raises possible confusion about which door the question is referring to. To address this and keeping in mind that we plan to exclude participants specifically if they believe that they cannot physically walk through the "low-cost" door, we only included the picture of the low-cost door with this question.
  Although the original study was conducted over MTurk (possibly from a more diverse sample), the data for the replication project will be collected from SONA (from UCSD undergraduate students). Aside from the exceptions listed above, we will be following the same analysis plans conducted in the original set of studies. The only other exception is that given that we will only be collecting data for the "low-cost" condition of Experiment 3a in our replication, we will compare the data from our replication project to the "no-cost" condition data collected in the original study.

## Results


### Data preparation

Data preparation following the analysis plan.
	
```{r include=F}
### Data Preparation

#### Load Relevant Libraries and Functions
library(lme4)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
```

```{r}
#### Import data
file_names <- dir("/Users/anlaha/Documents/PSY201B/GitHub/lopez-brau2023/data/pilot_a", full.names = TRUE) 

pilota <- do.call(rbind,lapply(file_names,read_csv))
```

```{r}
#### Data exclusion / filtering
pilota_mainqs = pilota %>%
  filter(question == "test" | question == "inclusion" | (question == "manipulation_check" & block == "exp3a")) %>%
  select(subject_id, block, object, question, correct)
```

```{r}
## cleaning all test trials
pilota_mainqs_wide = pilota_mainqs %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = question,
              values_from = correct)

##only including test from those who answered the inclusion question correctly and the manipulation check correctly for exp3a
pilota_pass = pilota_mainqs_wide %>%
  filter(inclusion == TRUE) %>%
  filter(manipulation_check == TRUE | is.na(manipulation_check)) 

#### Prepare data for analysis - create columns etc.
##pivoting longer - each row is each test question + marked correct or not
pilota_test = pilota_pass %>%
  select(!inclusion) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = "test",
               names_to = "TrialType",
               values_to = "Correct")

# code "1" for the "low-cost" door and "0" for the "no-cost" door (Exp 2) // code "1" for "should not walk through the door" and "0" for "should walk through the door" 
pilota_test = pilota_test %>%
  mutate(Response = ifelse(Correct == TRUE, "1", "0"))

#dataframe for exp 2 questions
pilota_exp2 = pilota_test %>%
  filter(block == "exp2")

#dataframe for exp 3 questions
pilota_exp3a = pilota_test %>%
  filter(block == "exp3a")
```

```{r}
## cleaning for binomial tests - only the first test trial
pilota_test1_qs = pilota_mainqs %>%
  distinct(subject_id, block, question, 
           .keep_all = TRUE)

pilota_test1_wide = pilota_test1_qs %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = question,
              values_from = correct)

##only including test from those who answered the inclusion question correctly and the manipulation check correctly for exp3a
pilota_test1_pass = pilota_test1_wide %>%
  filter(inclusion == TRUE)  %>%
  filter(manipulation_check == TRUE | is.na(manipulation_check)) 

# code "1" for the "low-cost" door and "0" for the "no-cost" door (Exp 2) // code "1" for "should not walk through the door" and "0" for "should walk through the door" 
pilota_test1 = pilota_test1_pass %>%
  mutate(Response = ifelse(test == TRUE, "1", "0"))

#exp 2 questions - only first test trial
pilota_exp2_test1 = pilota_test1 %>%
  filter(block == "exp2")

#exp 3 questions
pilota_exp3a_test1 = pilota_test1 %>%
  filter(block == "exp3a")
```

## Exp 2 questions: run binomial test comparing choices of "low-cost" door to chance
### compute bootstrapped 95% CIs
```{r}
pilota_exp2_test1_success = pilota_exp2_test1 %>%
  filter(Response == "1") 
  
success_exp2_test1 = as.numeric(count(pilota_exp2_test1_success))
exp2_test1_sample = as.numeric(nrow(pilota_exp2_test1))

exp2_binom = binom.test(success_exp2_test1, exp2_test1_sample, p = 0.5,
           alternative = "two.sided")
print(exp2_binom)
```

## Exp 3a "low-cost" questions: run binomial test comparing choices of door with object to chance
### compute bootstrapped 95% CIs
```{r}
pilota_exp3a_test1_success = pilota_exp3a_test1 %>%
  filter(Response == "1") 
  
success_exp3a_test1 = as.numeric(count(pilota_exp3a_test1_success))
exp3a_test1_sample = as.numeric(nrow(pilota_exp3a_test1))

exp3a_binom = binom.test(success_exp3a_test1, exp3a_test1_sample, p = 0.5,
           alternative = "two.sided")
print(exp3a_binom)
```
## Exp 3a comparison: run Fisher's test comparing choices of door with object in replicated "low-cost" to original "no-cost"
```{r}
# matrix with success on replication low-cost vs original no-cost
pilota_exp3a_comp <- matrix(c(success_exp3a_test1, 48, (exp3a_test1_sample - success_exp3a_test1), 32), 
                      nrow = 2,
                      dimnames = list(Condition = c("Low-cost", "No-cost"),
                                      Outcome = c("Success", "Failure")))

# Fisher's exact test
fisher.test(pilota_exp3a_comp)
```
